entries.title: Introducing the AlloyDB Omni web UI for easier cluster observability

entries.content:
Omkar Deshmukh

Product Manager

Josh Choinsky

Software Engineer

Managing PostgreSQL databases across on-premises, edge, and multi-cloud environments often forces administrators to rely on command-line tools, making it hard to see cluster health and quickly diagnose issues. To solve this, we are announcing the General Availability (GA) of the AlloyDB Omni Web UI for Red Hat and containers. This production-ready, read-only console gives you direct visibility into hardware telemetry, query performance, and configuration flags for AlloyDB Omni so you can troubleshoot workloads quickly and safely without leaving your local or enterprise environment.

What is AlloyDB Omni?

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, self-managed edition of AlloyDB that brings enterprise capabilities and full PostgreSQL compatibility to your own infrastructure. Built to run anywhere — across on-premises data centers, edge environments, and multi-cloud deployments — it includes built-in columnar acceleration and integrated AI tooling. With AlloyDB Omni, you can modernize demanding transactional and analytical workloads while retaining complete control over your operating environment.

Key Web UI capabilities at a glance

  • Cluster overview and profiles: Switch between target connection profiles quickly without using the command line.

  • System monitoring: View real-time performance telemetry for CPU, memory, and disk I/O to plan capacity and triage infrastructure issues.

  • Query performance: Identify resource-heavy SQL statements through a visual breakdown of database load, latency bottlenecks, and slow queries.

  • Columnar Engine diagnostics: Track the in-memory columnar store, caching, and coverage to verify analytical query acceleration.

  • Parameter and flag auditing: Inspect runtime database parameters centrally to identify configuration drift against your organizational baselines.

  • AlloyDB AI and ecosystem shortcuts: Inspect vector search and AI workflows, and access quick launchpad shortcuts for ecosystem tools like pgBackRest.

Production-safe diagnostics and profile management

When you triage complex database workloads across bare-metal VMs, containers, or Kubernetes, you need a clear, isolated view of instance health. The Web UI provides a dedicated visual environment for this.

  • Profile management: Store and toggle between saved connection profiles for local development, staging, or production environments.

  • Read-only operations: The interface operates strictly in read-only mode, ensuring that diagnostic sessions cannot execute write commands or modify your underlying database configurations.

Dual-layer observability: System and query monitoring

To isolate production performance spikes, you need immediate visibility into both hardware health and SQL statement execution.

  • System monitoring: The Web UI integrates with standard Prometheus telemetry to show you real-time CPU use, memory allocation, storage I/O, and active connection trends.

  • Query monitoring: The dashboard automatically ranks execution-heavy SQL statements by total latency and call frequency. You can instantly isolate unindexed or resource-intensive queries to resolve issues faster.

System Insights and Query Insights in AlloyDB Omni Web UI

Real-time Columnar Engine diagnostics

AlloyDB Omni includes an advanced Columnar Engine that organizes frequently accessed data in memory, accelerating analytical queries significantly compared to standard PostgreSQL. The Web UI helps you monitor this feature directly:

  • Memory footprint tracking: Check real-time columnar memory consumption against your hardware limits.

  • Columnarization and cache coverage: See exactly which tables and columns are actively cached in memory to confirm your workloads are running as fast as possible.

AlloyDB AI and Columnar Engine Insights in AlloyDB Omni Web UI

Database flag and parameter auditing

Keeping database parameters uniform across distributed environments keeps your operations stable. The Web UI gives you a central catalog to inspect active database flags and runtime settings. You can verify node settings against your organizational policies without connecting to servers via SSH or parsing configuration files manually. If configuration drift is detected, changes should be applied via the authoritative provisioning workflow (e.g., updating Kubernetes CRDs/GitOps manifests, running Ansible playbooks, or using alloydbctl).

Database flags in AlloyDB Omni Web UI

Built-in AlloyDB AI and tooling hub

As you build generative AI applications on top of PostgreSQL, the Web UI gives you direct visibility into vector search workflows and AI model integrations. You can also quickly navigate to documentation and external ecosystem resources, including backup tools like pgBackRest, directly from the console's tooling hub.

Operational scope and prerequisites

We designed the AlloyDB Omni Web UI with clear operational boundaries so you can deploy it easily within enterprise security boundaries and air-gapped environments.

  • Non-Intrusive Monitoring: The interface operates with minimal permissions out of the box, preserving your existing command-line tools and CI/CD pipelines as the authoritative controls for cluster provisioning and administrative workflows.

  • Standard monitoring prerequisites: To see complete system hardware metrics, you need standard Prometheus monitoring configured within your host environment.

Get started

Ready to modernize your PostgreSQL workloads and get dedicated observability for your AlloyDB Omni cluster ?

  • Sign up for enterprise access:

  • To request access to RPM-based enterprise distributions, advanced tooling, and the Web UI, complete the sign-up form for RPM based deployment of AlloyDB Omni.

  • To request access to container-based enterprise distributions, advanced tooling, and the Web UI, complete the sign-up form for container-based deployment.

  • Install the Web UI: Follow the step-by-step installation instructions in the AlloyDB Omni documentation to deploy the AlloyDB Omni Web UI

  • For deployment using Red Hat RPM: Deploy via native RPM Package

  • For deployment using Docker or Podman: Deploy via container image

entries.title: Near-zero downtime upgrades: Announcing Cloud SQL for MySQL blue-green deployments
entries.summary: Keeping production databases on supported versions shouldn’t require giving up your weekend. To stay secure, compliant, and with the best performance and newest AI capabilities, organizations need to run on the latest database engine versions. Yet for many teams, major version upgrades mean weeks of cross-team coordination, negotiating narrow maintenance windows, and hours of application downtime.
entries.content:
Vinod Kumar Subramanian

Senior Product Manager, Cloud SQL

Itay Maoz

Senior Engineering Director, Cloud SQL

Keeping production databases on supported versions shouldn’t require giving up your weekend. To stay secure, compliant, and with the best performance and newest AI capabilities, organizations need to run on the latest database engine versions. Yet for many teams, major version upgrades mean weeks of cross-team coordination, negotiating narrow maintenance windows, and hours of application downtime. In an era where mission-critical applications and AI agents operate as 24/7 systems of action, even a brief maintenance outage can mean disrupted customer experiences and lost revenue.

To help, we are excited to announce the preview of fully managed blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL, starting with Cloud SQL for MySQL. You can now execute major version upgrades and configuration updates with minimal downtime via the Google Cloud console or automated CLI scripts. By continuously synchronizing a parallel environment, teams can safely test with production data before a seamless cutover — all while keeping the original database as a reliable safety net after the switchover.

Why the upgrade dilemma matters to your business

Putting off major version upgrades (like moving from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4) exposes you to security vulnerabilities and causes you to miss out on performance improvements and latest AI capabilities. To test changes and avoid in-place upgrade downtime, teams often turn to a blue-green deployment — testing changes on a separate, upgraded staging copy (green) alongside the live database (blue) and switching traffic over once it’s ready. However, manual blue-green setups are incredibly complex to build, synchronize, and safely cut over.

Cloud SQL’s fully managed blue-green deployments can turn your database upgrades from a high-risk weekend project into a predictable, low-downtime operation.

The technical differentiators

With Cloud SQL, managed blue-green deployments automate the entire lifecycle across three stages:

  • Blue environment (production): Your current primary Cloud SQL instance, which continues serving live application traffic without interruption.

  • Green environment (staging): A temporary clone of your blue instance that Cloud SQL upgrades to your target database version and keeps in sync via continuous replication.

  • Switchover: When you're ready to cut over, Cloud SQL briefly sets the blue instance to read-only, finishes the final data synchronization, and promotes the green instance to your new primary database.

Three notable capabilities make this release a game-changer for enterprise workloads:

  • Near-zero downtime cutover: The transition from the old version to the new version is incredibly fast. Organizations using Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus experience sub-second downtime for maintenance.

  • No application changes: When you trigger the switchover, Cloud SQL automatically transfers your existing database IP address, instance name, and backups to the new database. Your developers do not need to rewrite connection strings, modify configuration files, or update client applications.

  • Safe, real-data testing: You can run real application traffic and queries against the upgraded green environment to verify performance before going live. If you spot an issue, simply delete the deployment before switchover without touching your live database.

Simple to orchestrate, built to scale

Upgrading your database environment can now be initiated in just a few clicks within the console, or via a simple CLI script.

With near-zero downtime switchovers, this feature takes the risk out of database upgrades. By shifting maintenance from a weekend chore to a routine daytime task, your team can stay ahead of security lifecycles, unlock the latest AI-ready engine features, and focus on building features that drive business growth, not managing infrastructure risk.

Try it today

Near-zero downtime database upgrades are available in preview for Cloud SQL for MySQL standalone primary instances, including High Availability configurations, with support for PostgreSQL coming soon.

Get started today by visiting the Cloud SQL console or reviewing the step-by-step documentation.

entries.title: Behind the scenes, two months later: How we ship Google Agent Skills like products
entries.summary: In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills, covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates that every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons that we learned along the way. entries.content:
Remigiusz Samborski

Lead Developer Relations Engineer

In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills, covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates that every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons that we learned along the way. You can adopt similar gates and review rules in your own skill repository.

Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000. It now hosts over 170 skills from teams across Google, and we distribute them across multiple AI platforms.

Building agent skills for a single developer or a small project is straightforward. You write a 

SKILL.md
file, define a few instructions, test it manually, and it works. At our scale, manual workflows stop being effective. Unvetted edits can introduce subtle bugs, and it becomes difficult to catch issues before they reach users.

The core philosophy: Ship skills like products

One key lesson from my previous post: a skill is a living product, not a one-off document. In practice, that means we ship every skill update like a product release.

It's tempting to treat a skill as documentation. But documentation explains concepts to a human reader, while a skill steers an AI agent's reasoning loop, tool selection, and execution path. A misplaced phrase in a skill can cause an agent to invoke invalid command flags, enter an infinite loop, or waste tokens.

That makes every instruction edit a behavioral change. You wouldn't ship a product update without testing it, and the same goes for a skill. This principle drives three core requirements:

  • Strict semantic versioning: Every behavioral change requires an explicit version bump.

  • Deterministic automated validation: Linters and validators check every proposed change before a human or AI reviewer sees it.

  • Mandatory evaluation evidence: Every change includes an evaluation report. It compares the skill against its previous version, or—if the skill is new—against an agent without the skill.

Automated conformance gates: The pull request pipeline

In my previous post, I briefly listed the checks that every skill passes on check-in: linters, link checkers, and AI-assisted checklists. Here's what's inside them, plus two gates that I haven't covered before: semantic versioning and evaluation suite validation.

When an author submits a change to our internal skills repository, an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline triggers immediately. Before a skill is exported to GitHub, it must pass these six automated gates and receive human approval:

  • Structural conformance: Directory layout, allowed files, and taxonomy.

  • Skill linters: Frontmatter, folder naming, and Markdown rules.

  • Semantic versioning: Version bump for every behavioral change.

  • Evaluation suite: Valid eval suite and a fresh eval report.

  • Link validation: Links are valid.

  • AI review agent: Skill quality and design standards.

  • Human approval: Final approval from a human reviewer (a subject matter expert).

Structural conformance and skill linters

Our automated validation suite inspects every pull request for structural and syntactical correctness. Some of the rules include these requirements:

  • Folder name and metadata name must match.

  • SKILL.md
    and description length limits are enforced.

  • All required fields in the frontmatter 

    metadata
    are present.

  • Only a curated list of files and directories is allowed within a skill directory.

  • All Markdown files follow formatting rules.

  • The main 

    README.md
    file and the machine-readable 
    index.json
    registry are up to date.

Semantic versioning

Every skill declares a semantic version in its 

SKILL.md
frontmatter metadata:

First, our automated checks verify that the version is a quoted string. YAML parses unquoted values like 

2.0
as numbers, which causes unexpected parsing errors in tools that expect a string.

Second, the validator checks the version transition itself. New skills must start at 

1.0.0
, and any change to an existing skill's instructions, scripts, or references requires a version bump or the pull request is blocked. Standard reset rules apply: bumping 
MAJOR
(for example, 
1.4.2
to 
2.0.0
) resets 
MINOR
and 
PATCH
to 
0
, and bumping 
MINOR
(for example, 
1.4.2
to 
1.5.0
) resets 
PATCH
to 
0
.

Why enforce strict versioning if the agent only reads the Markdown instructions? The version number is for the developer and their package tooling, not for the model at runtime. Skills don't auto-update in the background, which means there's no network check or latency overhead each time an agent invokes a skill. Instead, explicit versions let developers compare their locally installed skills against the upstream catalog and decide when to pull changes—for example, by running the 

npx skills update
command. This versioning also supports workflows where teams want to lock a critical skill to a known-good version to guarantee reproducible agent behavior across their projects.

Evaluation suite validation

Our continuous evaluations (evals) compare agent performance with and without each skill. Those results are only as reliable as the evaluation suites behind them. If a suite contains broken file references or compound expectations, test results become noisy and untrustworthy.

Our validator parses each evaluation suite and the pull request description. Then it checks several strict invariants:

  • Resolution of file-based prompts: When a test prompt references a file (such as 

    @file:test_prompt.txt
    ), the validator confirms that the target file exists and that it isn't empty.

  • Atomic expectations: Each expectation must check exactly one criterion. The validator blocks compound expectations until authors split them. Lesson 2 later in this post shows why.

  • Duplicate detection: The validator flags duplicate test prompts and conflicting expectations within the same evaluation suite.

  • Mandatory evaluation report: Every pull request that modifies a skill must link to an evaluation report in its description.

  • Eval staleness check: Authors usually iterate on a pull request as reviewers leave feedback. The validator confirms that the linked report ran against the latest commit.

Link validation

Over 170 skills link to documentation for fast-evolving Google products, and those pages can move long after a skill passes review. Rather than waiting for users to report broken links, we validate links at two stages. Before merge, pull request checks verify all relative links, such as files in 

references/
.

Then, every Monday, a GitHub Actions workflow runs lychee across all external links in the public repository and it reports any broken links to skill owners for remediation.

AI review agent

Linters and schema validators catch syntactic errors, but they can't evaluate overall quality. They can't tell you if an instruction is confusing, if a reference guide is too verbose, or if a task should have been a bash script instead of a large language model (LLM) instruction.

To solve this, we integrated an AI review agent into our review pipeline. When a change affects a skill, the AI reviewer inspects it using a dedicated review skill. Yes, we use a skill to review skills.

Here are the core rules the AI reviewer evaluates. You can adopt these rules in your own skill development workflows.

1. Skill suitability and the deterministic trap

The first question our AI reviewer asks is simple: Does this task belong in an instruction?

We often see authors fall into the deterministic trap. They write rigid, numbered sequences of command-line interface (CLI) commands directly into Markdown text.

LLMs are probabilistic engines. If an operation requires a strict sequence of commands where a variation can cause an error, embedding those commands in the instruction text invites hallucinations.

Our AI reviewer enforces a clear boundary between deterministic and probabilistic logic. Rigid CLI sequences, JSON parsers, and deployment steps must live in executable scripts under 

scripts/
. Markdown instructions are reserved for tasks that require judgment, such as choosing an architecture, diagnosing error logs, or synthesizing code.

This rule complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) guidance that I shared last time: prefer remote MCP tools whenever possible. When you must fall back to CLI or API calls, wrap them in a script instead of spelling them out in the instructions.

2. The L1/L2/L3 modular architecture

Context windows are valuable. Loading a 2,000-line skill into an agent consumes context and degrades reasoning.

Our AI reviewer enforces a three-tier information hierarchy that follows the progressive disclosure model of Agent Skills:

  • Level 1 (Metadata): The YAML frontmatter (

    name
    , 
    description
    ). The agent uses this concise summary for discovery and routing.

  • Level 2 (Core instructions): The main 

    SKILL.md
    file. The body must stay compact (under 500 lines). It provides workflow overviews, decision trees, and guardrails.

  • Level 3 (Reference docs): Detailed API references, schemas, and other reference tables live in a 

    references/
    directory.

Our AI reviewer enforces two distinct rules for Level 3: flat directory structure and single-hop indirection. Keeping 

references/
flat (no subdirectories) is a repository convention that discourages sprawling documentation trees and makes file discovery simpler. More importantly for runtime performance, the reviewer blocks chained references, where 
SKILL.md
links to a reference file that links to yet another file. Each hop requires an extra tool call, adding latency and cost, and our evaluations showed that agents frequently stop before following a second level of chained references.

3. Non-interactive script design

When skills bundle helper scripts in 

scripts/
, we expect agents to execute them directly in terminal sandboxes.

Our AI reviewer flags any script that blocks on interactive prompts. Every script must accept inputs through command-line flags or environment variables, provide 

--help
documentation, and include a 
--dry-run
or confirmation flag for destructive operations. Scripts also need to separate output cleanly, writing structured data (usually JSON) to standard output and writing actionable error messages to standard error.

Example AI review checklist snippet

The review skill also checks frontmatter for spec compliance and discovery, and it turns the L1/L2/L3 architecture into concrete structure rules. Here's an excerpt from those criteria:

Human approval

After it passes all automated checks, every pull request must receive approval from a human reviewer. The reviewer is typically the skill's subject matter expert and, for new skills, a member of the Central Skills team.

Lessons learned from repository history

Six months of commit history and pull request discussions reveal several practical takeaways.

1. Scope CI checks carefully

Early in the project, we configured automated pull request checks with broad directory patterns.

One check required an approved bug tracking ticket on every change. Because the pattern matched too broadly, engineers making a one-line typo fix were blocked for missing a tracking ticket. Meanwhile, newly added skills in deeper subdirectories went uninspected.

Takeaway: Match automated check rules to specific file operations, such as added versus modified files, and verify exact path depths. Treat minor edits to existing skills differently from new skills.

2. Atomic expectations

When we started writing evaluation suites, we saw authors write compound expectations like this:

If the agent configured the region and lifecycle rules but missed the uniform access flag, the LLM-as-a-judge scorer returned inconsistent ratings.

Migrating to atomic expectations resolved the inconsistent ratings:

Takeaway: Check exactly one criterion per expectation. Atomic expectations make evaluation results clear, reliable, and debuggable.

3. Documentation drift happens fast

In a multi-contributor repository, documentation tables drift within days if maintained manually.

Takeaway: If you publish an index or catalog, never rely on contributors to update it manually. Instead, write a generator script and enforce it with a CI unit test. That's the origin of the 

README.md
and 
index.json
checks in our linters. Our 
index.json
even opens with a warning: "This file is generated. Do not edit it by hand."

4. Gate expensive LLM checks behind fast deterministic ones

Running full evaluation suites and an AI review agent on every change can get expensive fast, both in token usage and CI runtime—especially when authors push frequent small commits during review.

In our pipeline, fast deterministic checks run first. Structural conformance, skill linters, and semantic versioning act as blocking gates: if any of them fail, the pipeline stops immediately and it won't trigger the AI reviewer or evaluation checks until those issues are fixed.

Takeaway: Stage your pipeline so cheap, deterministic checks block broken changes before LLM-powered gates run. When you build a similar system, consider adding further cost guardrails, such as manual triggers for heavy checks (for example, a 

/run-evals
pull request comment) or only triggering automatic re-runs when the diff exceeds a specific threshold.

Conclusion

Building a scalable Agent Skills repository requires more than good prompt engineering. It requires solid developer infrastructure:

  • Ship skills like products: version, validate, and evaluate every change.

  • Enforce semantic versioning and atomic expectations with automated CI gates.

  • Use an AI reviewer to catch design anti-patterns, such as the deterministic trap.

  • Check links before merge and on a schedule.

Links and further reading

To get started with Google Agent Skills, check out these resources:

  • Google Agent Skills repo: github.com/google/skills

  • Previous post: Behind the scenes: How we build, test, and scale Google Agent Skills

  • Launch announcement: Level Up Your Agents: Announcing Google's Official Skills Repository

  • Skills tutorial: Introduction: What Are Google Cloud Agent Skills?

What's next?

If you found this post helpful, share it with your friends on social media and connect with me on LinkedIn, X, or Bluesky.

Thanks for reading!

entries.title: How to troubleshoot GKE workloads faster with VPC Flow Logs
entries.summary: Having visibility into your network traffic is essential to operating Kubernetes environments effectively. When a service slows down or loses connectivity, knowing who is talking to whom lets you narrow the problem down quickly. In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols. In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary. T
entries.content:
Nishant Kumar

Product Manager

Whitney Jenkins

Product Manager

Having visibility into your network traffic is essential to operating Kubernetes environments effectively. When a service slows down or loses connectivity, knowing who is talking to whom lets you narrow the problem down quickly. In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols. In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary. Their IP addresses change constantly as pods scale, crash, or move between nodes, so a raw log entry showing 10.4.2.18 talking to 10.4.8.44 tells you little about which workload (and pod) owned that address, what namespace it was in, or what application it was trying to reach. By the time you search your cluster, the pod may already be gone!

In a Google Cloud environment, VPC Flow Logs closes this gap at the network layer. Google Cloud's virtual network already sees every connection a pod makes, so each sampled flow is recorded with the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) metadata behind the IP address: pod, workload, namespace, and service. You get workload-level attribution for L3/L4 traffic without deploying extra agents or sidecars, and it complements in-cluster Container Network Interface (CNI) and dataplane observability tools you may already run when you need deeper detail. Let’s take a deeper look at how VPC Flow Logs and GKE work together, and how to get started with it.

How GKE metadata enriches VPC Flow Logs

VPC Flow Logs samples traffic directly inside Google Cloud's virtual network. When flow logs are enabled for a subnet that hosts a GKE cluster, every record of pod traffic that passes through the VPC network is annotated with the Kubernetes context that owned the IP address at the time of sampling. This helps ensure the context is preserved even after the pod is gone:

  • Cluster: The cluster name and location.

  • Workload: The pod name and namespace, along with the controller that owns the pod, such as a deployment, StatefulSet, or DaemonSet.

  • Service name: The Kubernetes service that received the traffic.

  • Node and zone: The standard VPC fields, including the node VM and its zone on both ends of the flow.

If you register your GKE workloads in App Hub, each record also carries application-level labels (

apphubSource
and 
apphubDestination
) that identify the business application, environment, and criticality of each endpoint. This is especially useful when GKE microservices talk to App Hub-registered resources outside the cluster, such as Cloud Run services.

Before you start

Upgrade your log bucket to Observability Analytics (formerly Log Analytics): Flow Analyzer reads only from an upgraded bucket, typically 

_Default
. Note: This upgrade is permanent.

gcloud logging buckets update _Default \
    --location=global \
    --enable-analytics

Enable VPC Flow Logs organization-wide: One organization-level configuration covers every subnet in every VPC network, including future clusters (requires Network Management Admin role). Keep 

include-all-metadata
on so every record carries namespace and pod details. To balance visibility against cost, you can add a secondary sampling rate (
--flow-sampling
), an aggregation interval (
--aggregation-interval
), or a filter expression (
--filter-expr
) to view only the traffic of interest.

gcloud network-management vpc-flow-logs-configs create CONFIG_NAME \
    --location=global \
    --organization=ORGANIZATION_ID \
    --metadata=include-all-metadata

Turn on intranode visibility: Autopilot clusters already have it, but you need to enable it on Standard clusters. Note: Enabling it restarts control plane and node components and adds some per-node overhead, so test it on a non-production cluster first.

gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER_NAME \
    --location=LOCATION \
    --enable-intra-node-visibility

Now you’re ready to get started.

Analyze traffic visually in Flow Analyzer

VPC Flow Logs write every record to Cloud Logging, you can search and query it in Logs Explorer or Log Analytics. For day-to-day work, Flow Analyzer, part of Network Intelligence Center, turns the same records into an interactive chart and table, so you can group and filter traffic by cluster, namespace, workload, pod, or service in a few clicks. 

The walkthroughs below use Online Boutique, an open-source microservices demo, on a GKE Autopilot cluster in us-central1. A 

loadgenerator
deployment sends synthetic shopper traffic to the 
frontend
, which calls 
productcatalogservice
, 
cartservice
, 
currencyservice
, 
recommendationservice
, 
shippingservice
, 
adservice
, and 
checkoutservice
. 

Case 1: Turn IP addresses into workload names

Whether you’re investigating an incident or assessing an architecture change, the first question is always the same: Which endpoints are communicating, and at what volume?

Rather than presenting ephemeral IP address pairs, GKE metadata allows Flow Analyzer to answer this question directly using Kubernetes workload names.

Steps in Flow Analyzer:

  • Open Network Intelligence Center > Flow Analyzer and set the time range to last 1 hour.

  • Under Source and Destination, set Organize flows by to GKE workload.

  • In the filter bar, add the GKE workload is known filter so only pod-to-pod traffic is shown.

  • Click Run new query.

Grouping traffic by Source GKE workload and Destination GKE workload in Flow Analyzer to map microservice dependencies without raw IP lookups.

Key insights: Sorted by volume, the table is a ready-made application dependency map: 

frontend
handles incoming requests from 
loadgenerator
(representing user traffic), while 
productcatalogservice
answers calls from both 
recommendationservice
and 
frontend
. Because each row shows workload names instead of raw IP addresses, any unauthorized or unexpected workload-to-workload communication immediately becomes apparent.

Case 2: Drill into a single service

When a service is slow or about to change, you need to know who depends on it and how heavily.

Steps in Flow Analyzer:

  • Change Traffic aggregation to Client ↔ server (bidirectional), so requests and responses between a pair are counted together.

  • Under Server, add the filter GKE workload = 

    productcatalogservice
    .

  • Click Run new query, then click Details on the top row.

Filtering on Server GKE workload (productcatalogservice) with Client ↔ server (bidirectional) aggregation to view caller share and the Details timeline.

Key insights: You get every caller of the catalog service, each caller's share of its traffic, and a timeline for every pair, so if one caller's line climbs while the others stay flat, you know where to look first. When the question is latency rather than volume, switch the display mode to latency to rank the same callers by round-trip time.

Case 3: Find the pods that talk across zones

In a regional GKE cluster, chatty services that land in different zones send every request across a zone boundary, adding inter-zone data transfer charges. Because VPC Flow Logs record the zone at both ends of every flow, the pod pairs driving that traffic are easy to spot.

Steps in Flow Analyzer:

  • Switch from Basic filters to SQL filters, which let you compare two fields of the same flow.

  • In the WHERE box, enter 

    src_gcp_zone <> dest_gcp_zone
    .

  • Set Organize flows by to Source GCP zone, Source GKE pod, Destination GCP zone, and Destination GKE pod.

  • Click Run new query.

Using SQL filters with src_gcp_zone <> dest_gcp_zone and multi-attribute grouping to identify pod pairs driving cross-zone network traffic.

Key insights: The table displays cross-zone traffic ranked by volume, identifying the exact pods and zones on each end. In our cluster, the top flows occur between a 

frontend
pod in us-central1-b and a 
currencyservice
pod in us-central1-c, followed by 
checkoutservice
, 
shippingservice
, and 
productcatalogservice
pairs. To investigate further, click Explore in Log Analytics to open the underlying SQL query for additional customization, such as adding joins or time buckets.

GKE has a built-in answer: set 

trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
(
PreferClose
on older versions) on the Service to prefer healthy endpoints in the caller's zone, and make sure each zone has enough replicas to serve its own traffic.

What to keep in mind

  • Pod-to-internet traffic: VPC Flow Logs carry no pod annotations, because the masquerade agent replaces the pod IP with the node IP before the flow is sampled. Keeping internal destinations in the non-masquerade list preserves pod names for those flows, and if you run 

    ip-masq-agent
    with intranode visibility, that list must also include the cluster's node and pod IP ranges to avoid connectivity problems.

  • Blocked traffic: Traffic blocked by a network policy never reaches the VPC network, so use NetworkPolicy logging to investigate it.

  • Sampling: Flow logs are sampled, which makes byte and packet counts well suited for ranking and trending rather than per-connection accounting.

Next steps

If your clusters already have VPC Flow Logs turned on, upgrading the

entries.title: How GKE networking scales to support high densities of concurrent AI agents
entries.summary: What do you need to orchestrate high-density concurrent AI agents? As we transition from static requests toward autonomous agentic workflows, the need for secure, high-density sandboxes is pushing conventional infrastructure far beyond its architectural breaking point. This transition is driving top-tier research labs to demand infrastructure at unprecedented scale — often up to one million concur
entries.content:
Srini Jasti

Group Product Manager

Venkat Krishnan

Software Engineer

What do you need to orchestrate high-density concurrent AI agents? As we transition from static requests toward autonomous agentic workflows, the need for secure, high-density sandboxes is pushing conventional infrastructure far beyond its architectural breaking point. This transition is driving top-tier research labs to demand infrastructure at unprecedented scale — often up to one million concurrent code-execution sandboxes!

At this scale, the efficiency of your Kubernetes networking infrastructure directly impacts the economic viability of an agentic initiative. In advanced workflows like reinforcement learning (RL), extreme pod churn can mean thousands of isolated sandboxes spinning up and down every minute. To make sure that valuable GPUs and TPUs are spending their time executing models rather than waiting on sandboxes to initialize, you need sub-second provisioning and extreme compute density.

By providing secure, lightweight isolation, Agent Sandbox on GKE is uniquely positioned to power these highly dynamic execution environments. Furthermore, for next-generation workloads with millions of concurrent idle sessions, Agent Substrate on GKE builds on these primitives to deliver even greater density and sub-second state rehydration.

In this post, you will learn how GKE Dataplane V2 optimizes network identity management, solves identity scaling limits, and enables sub-second provisioning to power high-density, large-scale AI agent workloads.

A common scale challenge: network identity management

Operating with massive concurrency introduces fascinating new engineering challenges, particularly in how you manage network identities. Traditionally, custom controllers and workload orchestrators often assign unique, dynamic labels to each pod (such as agent-id, timestamps, or claim-uid). GKE Dataplane V2, powered by eBPF technology, helps enforce robust network security policies by mapping pod labels to a numeric identity. Because agentic workflows generate highly unique labels for every pod, the system proactively provisions a distinct identity for each sandbox. In a rapidly changing environment, this serial allocation process can briefly pause pod creation as the system securely updates eBPF maps, occasionally leading to slower-than-desired initialization. Additionally, sophisticated workloads can approach the cluster-wide limit of 65,536 network identities, either through this rapid generation or overall scale of the workload itself.

GKE network dataplane innovations for an agentic world

Providing a reliable and highly secure platform is fundamental to everything we do. As such, we needed to find a way to provide the same underlying identity and security controls while providing higher scalability and performance. That's where the architectural innovations in GKE Dataplane V2 come in. A customer has testified to the success of Agent Substrate on GKE to orchestrate hundreds of thousands of secure environments across clusters and handle spikes of over 30,000 sandboxes on a single cluster. 

To achieve this, GKE relies on a two-pronged networking approach:

Migrating high-cardinality data

Google's GKE Dataplane V2 separates "identifying" data from "functional" metadata. Ensure your fields that do not actively participate in service selector matching or core resource grouping are migrated from the Pod's Labels set to the Annotations set. GKE Dataplane V2 intelligently calculates network identities based on labels rather than annotations, moving this high-cardinality metadata out of the labels completely bypasses the need for per-Pod identity generation. This elegant shift natively resolves identity scaling limits without sacrificing visibility.

Advanced Cilium label filtering

In addition, applying precise label exclusion filters (e.g., using the cilium-config-emergency-override ConfigMap in kube-system) by configuring rules like !agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash or !timestamp, these explicitly instruct GKE Dataplane V2  to gracefully ignore these dynamic labels during security identity calculation.

This means that even if a developer framework inadvertently introduces high-cardinality labels, configuring appropriate exclusion filters allows Google’s network dataplane to drop them automatically.

As a result, identical agent types continue sharing a single Cilium pod identity, maintaining the ultra-low-latency startup times critical for dynamic AI workloads. By preventing linear identity growth and avoiding Cilium’s 65,536 identity limit, GKE provides leading speed and efficiency for fully isolated agents with 300 sandboxes per second at sub-second latency.

Looking ahead

For workloads that require extreme performance, scale, and density, Agent Substrate natively integrates these GKE Dataplane V2 recommendations while bypassing Kubernetes scheduling limits, pushing GKE’s performance and scale even further. In benchmark validation running 200,000 agents, Agent Substrate sustained 500 activations per second at less than 500 ms suspend and resume latency. You can deploy it on your existing GKE clusters today to minimize idle compute costs for your most demanding AI workflows.

By optimizing network identity calculation and filtering high-cardinality metadata, GKE Dataplane V2 addresses critical infrastructure bottlenecks in large-scale AI workloads. These architectural improvements reduce sandbox provisioning latency to sub-second levels, minimize expensive GPU idle times, and help maintain high compute density. Ultimately, these efficiencies let you scale your agentic AI operations reliably while controlling operational costs.

To learn more, explore Agent Sandbox and Agent Substrate on GKE.

entries.title: Step into a new dimension with XREAL AURA, the first-of-its-kind wired XR glasses
entries.summary: The world of work is rapidly evolving, and with it, the tools we use to stay productive and connected. As AI adoption transforms daily workflows, form factors like XR headsets and glasses offer fresh ways to reimagine how productive work happens across apps and devices.Today marks the launch of XREAL AURA, a first-of-kind set of wired XR glasses built on Android XR. XREAL AURA’s form factor brings
entries.content:
Will Ro

Head of Product Operations, Google

Sean Ginevan

Head of Technology Partnerships, Google

Android XR

Android XR is an AI-powered operating system that blends digital information with the real world. Available now on headsets and coming soon to glasses, it's designed to help you watch, work, explore, and play like never before.

Learn more

The world of work is rapidly evolving, and with it, the tools we use to stay productive and connected. As AI adoption transforms daily workflows, form factors like XR headsets and glasses offer fresh ways to reimagine how productive work happens across apps and devices.

Today marks the launch of XREAL AURA, a first-of-kind set of wired XR glasses built on Android XR. XREAL AURA’s form factor brings new and impressive features for enterprises such as:

  • Spatial computing on wired glasses using a newly introduced split-compute architecture.
  • An optical-see-through display with a 70-degree field of view that layers rich visual content directly onto your physical world, allowing you to stay connected.
  • A glasses frame weight of less than 95g, allowing for extended work sessions by employees.

Most importantly, AURA brings unique productivity benefits to users. Employees will have out-of-the-box support for enterprise apps, including popular titles currently available on the Google Play Store. And if the hundreds of Android productivity titles aren’t enough, you can also connect your laptop and bring those applications into your spatial environment as well. AURA’s displayport-in (DP-in) function makes it seamless to connect laptops across platforms directly alongside Android apps.

Management and security of Android XR devices are crucial for IT teams. We introduced Android Enterprise management on Android XR earlier this year, and XREAL AURA devices will be managed through the same framework. Key management and security features include:

  • Managed Google Play: Securely distribute and manage public and private business apps, to ensure that end users have all the tools they need.
  • Android zero-touch enrollment: Automatically deploy Android devices remotely out-of-the-box, to save time and enable enrollment at scale.
  • Device management: Support of fully managed device mode, to support configuration of core system resources like Wi-Fi, as well the ability to set system policies like disallowing apps.
  • Google Play Protect: Defend against threats with proactive machine-learning powered detection of malware, phishing and ransomware.
  • Core Android platform security: Multi-layered protections spanning from hardware to OS, with verified boot, and device encryption that keep devices protected from emerging threats with regular and modular security updates from Google.
  • Device Trust from Android Enterprise: Secures devices, respects privacy, and empowers employees to work from anywhere, including devices that may not be managed.

XREAL AURA allows users to easily see both the world around them as well as digital data at the same time. Because of its unique form factor, users can seamlessly switch between extended reality and interacting with their physical space. This unlocks new use cases for enterprise users that include:

  • Offering spatial productivity across virtual monitors visible only to the user and with 3D content
  • Getting help from virtual experts while working on a piece of equipment
  • Easily visualizing complex information on top of physical spaces
  • Designing and simulating products in 3D
  • Using voice to easily guide information from the physical world into digital systems of record

Android XR brings advanced computing and AI to daily work through powerful devices like the XREAL AURA wired glasses, all seamlessly managed by the secure and familiar Android Enterprise framework. This holistic approach ensures businesses can harness the full potential of XR today.

Interested to find out more about Android or have follow up questions, let us know in the Customer Community.

For more information on how XREAL AURA can transform the way you work, watch, and play, check out the For more information on how XREAL AURA can transform the way you work, watch, and play, check out the News from Google blog.

To purchase the device, check out the XREAL AURA shop.

XREAL AURA is only available for use by users in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. Additionally, it is only available for ages 18+. Some apps and features require download, setup, or subscription

entries.title: Introducing VMware solution on Google Cloud
entries.summary: Many organizations with workloads on VMware are looking for ways to expedite their data center exits, migrate and modernize their mission-critical workloads, or simply leverage the cloud as a secondary disaster recovery site. But they want to do so without altering existing operational playbooks. Today, we are announcing the general availability of the VMware solution on Google Cloud, part of the
entries.content:
Sunny Dua

Group Product Manager

Prashanth Bungale

Director, Product Management

VMware solution on Google Cloud provides customers with more options to transform their VMware estate

Many organizations with workloads on VMware are looking for ways to expedite their data center exits, migrate and modernize their mission-critical workloads, or simply leverage the cloud as a secondary disaster recovery site. But they want to do so without altering existing operational playbooks.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of the VMware solution on Google Cloud, part of the Google Cloud Modernize portfolio, giving you full administrative authority for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) on dedicated Google Cloud bare metal.

This new deployment model complements our existing Google-managed service, offering you greater flexibility and architectural choice for running VMware workloads in Google Cloud. With this new self managed offering, organizations with dedicated operational practices maintain direct control over their virtualization stack, specific maintenance windows, and custom integration with third-party monitoring and management tools.

The launch of VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x by Broadcom is a key driver behind this self-managed deployment option. Featuring a unified VCF control plane for end-to-end stack deployment and lifecycle management, this solution enables Google Cloud customers to directly leverage Broadcom's latest innovations and fully maximize their licensing investments in VMware Cloud Foundation.

“Customers want the agility of Google Cloud without rearchitecting their VMware environments or abandoning the operational practices they have invested in. With the new VMware solution on Google Cloud, VCF license portability allows customers to bring their existing subscriptions and run their VMware workloads unchanged, with complete administrative control on dedicated Z3 bare metal and the ability to apply Google Cloud commitments and discounts to optimize their costs.” - Abhay Kumar, Global Head of Hyperscalers, VMware Cloud Foundation Division, Broadcom

Expanding deployment choices for VMware workloads

When it comes to VMware workloads, Google Cloud now offers two distinct choices tailored to your priorities, letting you choose the operational model that matches your workloads’ characteristics and the levels of control you need: Google Cloud VMware Engine, and the VMware solution on Google Cloud.

High-performance architecture on bare metal

The self-managed VMware solution is deployed on dedicated GCE Z3 bare metal instances (z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal). Powered by 2.2 GHz - 4th Generation Intel Xeon Processors (Sapphire Rapids) processors, each node delivers:

  • 96 physical cores (192 hyper-threads)

  • 1.5 TB RAM

  • 72 TB all-flash NVMe storage

  • 200 Gbps networking

Operating natively within Google Cloud alongside GCE and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), this architecture provides high bandwidth and low-latency networking for transactional databases and direct access to native Google Cloud services, including BigQuery, the Gemini platform, Cloud Run, and more.

The solution's storage architecture is built on VMware vSAN hyperconverged infrastructure using high-performance, all-flash NVMe storage from Z3 nodes. Beyond standard storage, these drives can also be utilized for NVMe memory tiering. In addition to vSAN, the solution also supports NetApp volumes.

"VMware solution on Google Cloud gives enterprises greater control, choice, and architectural freedom as they move to the cloud. We are excited to expand our partnership with Google Cloud by offering NetApp Volumes as an external datastore. Together, we’re helping customers confidently migrate their VMware workloads and data to Google Cloud while retaining the flexibility, performance and data management capabilities they rely on.” - Pravjit Tiwana, SVP/GM, Cloud Storage, NetApp

Realizing clear customer value and TCO optimization

Pairing VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 with Google Cloud’s Z3 bare metal infrastructure delivers significant economic and operational efficiency:

  • Commercial flexibility and BYOL: Bring portable Broadcom VCF subscriptions while allocating Google Cloud commitments and Flexible Committed Use Discounts (Flex CUDs) toward Z3 bare metal shapes.

  • NVMe memory tiering: Tiering between DDR memory (Tier 0) and high-speed local NVMe (Tier 1) can reduce server TCO by up to 40%.

  • vSAN Express Storage Architecture (ESA): Utilizing high-throughput local NVMe storage reduces storage TCO by up to 39% compared to traditional external arrays.

  • Active live patching: Up to 80% live patching coverage for critical security updates reduces planned maintenance downtime.

Architectural and commercial differentiation

In addition to the above-mentioned benefits, Google Cloud provides distinct operational and technical advantages that go beyond standard cloud hosting:

  • Triple-governance operational choices: Select from Google-, customer-, or partner- frameworks to align precisely with your operating model.

  • Granular capacity sizing: Access bare metal shapes across GCE hardware families to optimize utilization resulting in a lower TCO.

  • Global virtual networking: Peer complex multi-edge and multi-VPC topologies natively via Andromeda and Network Connectivity Center (NCC).

  • AI Acceleration: Seamlessly connect systems of record directly to BigQuery and Gemini platform to enable AI capabilities.

What our customers are saying

“Our early assessment shows significant potential. Separating the hardware lifecycle from the virtualization layer gives us the ability to scale bare-metal capacity in minutes, while still retaining full administrative control. This provides the flexibility of the cloud with the level of control we require from our infrastructure platforms.” - Scott Ronan, Senior Director of Platforms, Databases & Cloud, GXO Logistics

Partner-managed ecosystem

For organizations that prefer managed services, Google Cloud partners with organizations with expertise across both Google Cloud and VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) to provide end-to-end support for self-managed VMware solution including:

  • Day 0: Architecture planning and solution design

  • Day 1: Deployment and migration execution

  • Day 2 and beyond: Ongoing lifecycle management and operations

Delivered via professional or managed services contracts, you can collaborate with your preferred providers or tap into our featured partner offerings on the self-managed VMware solution: Accenture, Advanced Business Computing, Cognizant, Devoteam, HCL, IBM, Infosys, Insight, LiverX, ModernZ, Pellera, Quantiphi, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, and Xtravirt.

Getting started

VMware solution on Google Cloud is generally available across 22 Google Cloud regions, with planned expansion to more regions in upcoming quarters.

To get started:

  • Visit the VMware solution on Google Cloud webpage for more details.

  • Review the solution overview and core concepts on the documentation page.

  • Reach out to your Google Cloud account team or an authorized partner to evaluate this offering.

entries.title: Powering the agentic enterprise with latest innovations in Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud
entries.summary: For decades, core enterprise operations — from global supply chains and financial ledgers to billing engines — have relied on the performance and transactional integrity of Oracle databases. Today at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, Google Cloud and Oracle are expanding our partnership across the AI stack — spanning AI compute and infrastructure (including making Google TPUs available through Oracle
entries.content:
Kiran Shenoy

Outbound Product Manager, Databases

Kunal Agarwal

Product Manager, Databases

For decades, core enterprise operations — from global supply chains and financial ledgers to billing engines — have relied on the performance and transactional integrity of Oracle databases. Today at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, Google Cloud and Oracle are expanding our partnership across the AI stack — spanning AI compute and infrastructure (including making Google TPUs available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure), enterprise data, and agentic AI — by deepening the integration between Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud, Google’s Agentic Data Cloud, and Gemini.

By unifying Oracle’s mission-critical operational data and applications with Google Cloud’s data and AI ecosystem — including BigQuery and Gemini models — enterprises can move beyond static analytics and build autonomous, agentic workflows. This architecture breaks down traditional data silos, giving agents direct, secure, and real-time access to the foundational enterprise data required to drive real-world action.

Foundational building blocks for agentic AI

To unlock production-grade agentic AI, enterprises need more than raw model capability — they need strong database connectivity, unified data governance, and rich semantic context working together as a cohesive foundation. First announced at Google Cloud Next '26, the following core capabilities serve as the building blocks for building conversational intelligence, end-to-end governance, and autonomous agent environments on Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud:

  • Remote MCP Server with Data API: The Remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server for Oracle workloads — powered by the IAM-governed ExecuteSQL Data API — is now generally available. Together, they provide a unified, standardized interface that enables AI agents, Google Cloud services, and enterprise applications to securely run SQL and interact directly with Oracle databases. By resolving database credentials automatically through Secret Manager and enforcing Google Cloud IAM policies, this capability eliminates the need for custom natural-language-to-SQL middleware, bastion VMs, or plaintext passwords.

  • Knowledge Catalog integration: Google Cloud’s Knowledge Catalog integration, currently in preview, unifies enterprise metadata discovery and governance across Oracle databases and the broader Google Agentic Data Cloud. By automatically cataloging schemas and business metadata, organizations can enforce consistent access controls, track data provenance, and supply the rich semantic context that agents require to reason accurately over complex operational data. Click here to sign-up for this feature.

Gemini connector for Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud

Building directly on the foundational capabilities discussed above, we’re also announcing the preview of Gemini connector for Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud. With this native integration, business users and developers can interact directly with their Oracle databases on Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud using natural language queries right inside the Gemini app. Behind the scenes, Gemini automatically leverages Knowledge Catalog to discover, search, and ground responses strictly in the governed Oracle data each user is authorized to access — turning complex operational databases into an intuitive, conversational experience without compromising enterprise security. Click here to sign-up for this feature. 

Oracle in Gemini and Gemini in Oracle

Beyond direct database queries, Google Cloud and Oracle are connecting agentic workflows across the broader application layer — bringing Oracle data into Gemini and embedding Gemini models natively inside Oracle applications:

  • Oracle in Gemini: Available today, Oracle in Gemini introduces conversational analytics, cross-cloud database connectors, and domain-aware agents — including the new Oracle AI Database Agent in Gemini. Anchored by over 135 pre-built operational and developer skills and standardized MCP connectivity with zero plaintext credentials, enterprises can orchestrate multi-agent workflows across JD Edwards, E-Business Suite, NetSuite, and Oracle Fusion without custom SQL or brittle middleware.

  • Gemini models in Oracle applications: Concurrently, Gemini frontier reasoning is embedded directly into Oracle Fusion AI Agent Studio, Fusion Claw, Oracle Fusion Applications, and NetSuite — combining Oracle database intelligence with Gemini’s agentic capabilities to automate execution across transactional systems of record.

  • Partner-ready agentic blueprints: To help organizations rapidly deploy these governed workflows, Google Cloud and Oracle are collaborating with leading partners and global systems integrators — including Argano, Automus, Calfus, HCL, IBM, Infosys, LTM, Pythian, TCS, and Tessell — who provide pre-built operational skills, custom MCP connectors, and industry blueprints for production-grade agentic architectures.

Empowering choice with lakehouse, streaming, and federation

Every enterprise has distinct architectural priorities, latency thresholds, and governance requirements when connecting operational Oracle data to BigQuery and AI workloads. Rather than prescribing a one-size-fits-all integration pattern, Google Cloud and Oracle offer a complete spectrum of data unification choices so customers can select — or combine — the exact approach that best fits their workload and use case:

Bi-directional Google Cloud borderless Lakehouse and Oracle AI Lakehouse

Modern enterprise data architectures are increasingly multi-cloud and grounded in open standards. Building on our strategic partnership, Google Cloud and Oracle delivered a key innovation earlier this year to support cross-cloud data interoperability powered by open Apache Iceberg standard: integrating Google’s borderless Lakehouse with Oracle AI Lakehouse.

This work enabled the borderless Lakehouse to read Apache Iceberg tables created by Oracle AI Lakehouse across any public cloud or on-premises environment, leveraging catalogs and storage supported by both platforms.

Today, we are advancing it further by making it fully bi-directional with Oracle Access to Google Cloud borderless Lakehouse (preview). Now, Oracle Autonomous AI Database and Google’s borderless Lakehouse (powered by BigQuery and Managed Spark) can directly query and execute write/DML operations on shared Apache Iceberg tables in Google Cloud Storage, completely eliminating the need for ETL or data replication.

By utilizing a Lakehouse runtime REST catalog integrated into Oracle via DBMS_CATALOG, this bi-directional integration delivers an open-standards storage framework while empowering analytical teams (using BigQuery and Gemini) and operational teams (using Oracle SQL) to collaborate over a single, unified source of truth. You can click here to sign-up for this feature.

Sub-second CDC streaming with OCI GoldenGate

For organizations that prefer to continuously reflect mission-critical operational data inside BigQuery for high-scale analytics and AI, real-time change data capture (CDC) provides an immediate competitive edge. Through native OCI GoldenGate integration, CDC events are extracted directly from Oracle redo logs without touching table blocks or adding overhead to transactional workloads. Transactions stream securely across Google Cloud private networks straight into BigQuery managed tables, delivering sub-second analytical freshness to power Gemini, feature stores, and live business intelligence dashboards, while also streamlining migrations from on-premises environments to Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud.

BigQuery query federation with Oracle

When workloads call for on-demand operational visibility or infrequent cross-estate joins without moving data, BigQuery query federation with Oracle, in preview, enables real-time, in-place analytics directly against live Oracle databases. Using the EXTERNAL_QUERY function, data teams can execute native Oracle SQL directly from BigQuery queries, dashboards, and pipelines to retrieve live transactional records and join them easily with petabyte-scale BigQuery datasets. This zero-copy approach simplifies operations and lowers Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) by eliminating duplicate storage and ETL maintenance for ad-hoc lookups, intraday risk reporting, and live fraud detection. Please reach out to your Google Cloud account team if you want to sign-up for this feature.

Global expansion and public sector compliance

We continue to expand the global physical footprint and compliance boundaries of Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud to meet customers wherever they operate, with new regions and certifications.

  • The 

    europe-west12-a
    (Turin, Italy) and 
    northamerica-south1-b
    (Queretaro, Mexico) regions are now live, joining global hubs including Milan, Iowa, São Paulo, Tokyo, Sydney, and Mumbai to deliver ultra-low-latency access and local data residency.

FedRAMP High certification

  • At Oracle AI World, Oracle announced plans to pursue FedRAMP High certification for Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud. This initiative will allow US government and public sector entities to run regulated workloads using Oracle Exadata Database Service on dedicated infrastructure within Google Cloud Assured Workloads.

  • Operating inside a FedRAMP High-authorized environment enables federal agencies to safeguard sensitive, unclassified data while co-locating Oracle workloads with existing applications and Gemini. Agencies can access live Oracle data with minimal latency, streamlined billing, and simplified procurement via Google Cloud Marketplace or certified partners — all within their compliance boundaries.

Building the agentic future

By combining Oracle’s proven transactional engine with Google’s Agentic Data Cloud, enterprise data transitions from passive systems of record into an active, intelligent operational engine. Whether unifying data through open Apache Iceberg lakehouses, streaming sub-second changes via GoldenGate, federating live queries from BigQuery, or conversing directly with governed Oracle data through Gemini, organizations now have the complete flexibility and security required to deploy autonomous AI agents at scale — driving predictive insights and automated actions across their most critical business processes.

Get started today

Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud is available directly through the Google Cloud Marketplace, allowing you to deploy using your existing Google Cloud commitments, unified billing, and Oracle Support Rewards.

To explore further, visit the Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud overview, dive into the official Oracle Database@Google Cloud Documentation, or reach out to your Google Cloud account team to schedule an architecture briefing.

entries.title: Securely connecting Gemini Enterprise to Snowflake data
entries.summary: Enterprise AI needs to go beyond simple chat interfaces. To provide real value, AI agents must access your data warehouses to generate actionable insights, all while maintaining strict security and data governance.This guide explores how to build a secure bridge between Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise and Snowflake. By using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Google Agent Development Kit (A
entries.content:
Pankaj Bajpai

Cloud Data Engineer

Abhilash Adavi

AI Engineer

Enterprise AI needs to go beyond simple chat interfaces. To provide real value, AI agents must access your data warehouses to generate actionable insights, all while maintaining strict security and data governance.

This guide explores how to build a secure bridge between Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise and Snowflake. By using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK), you can empower your agent to act as an assistant that understands natural language, generates precise SQL via Snowflake Cortex and executes queries with user-level permissions.

Choosing the right integration pattern

Direct Connection vs. custom orchestration

The Google ADK architecture demonstrated in this post represents the advanced / custom orchestration pattern. It is designed for developers building complex, multi-agent systems on Google Cloud, such as workflows that combine Snowflake insights with external enterprise tools, custom reasoning loops, or cross-platform state management in Gemini Agent Engine.

For standard enterprise basic use cases where you want to connect Gemini Enterprise directly to Snowflake use the joint solutions mentioned in this link.

The architectural approach

This architecture allows a business user to ask questions like, "What were our top 5 selling items in Texas last quarter?"

Rather than exposing raw SQL execution to the client, the agent delegates both query generation and execution to a governed Snowflake Cortex Agent exposed through the Snowflake MCP server:

  • Governed translation: The ADK agent passes the user's natural language question to the Snowflake MCP server, which invokes the Cortex Agent (CORTEX_AGENT_RUN) backed by Cortex Analyst semantic view.
  • Direct execution within the governed boundary: The Cortex Agent translates the question into SQL and executes it directly inside Snowflake using the authenticated user's OAuth session and role privileges, returning the structured results to the ADK agent.

This approach provides deterministic text-to-SQL translation mapped to your corporate semantic definitions, keeps query execution inside Snowflake's governed boundary, and reduces the risk of schema hallucinations or unvalidated SQL execution.

System architecture flow

The diagram below illustrates the trust boundaries and the numbered flow of execution between the Gemini Enterprise app and Snowflake ecosystems.

Detailed execution sequence

To highlight how the agent delegates natural language query translation and governed execution to the Snowflake Cortex Agent over MCP, see the sequence diagram below:

Step 1: Setting up the Snowflake security integration

A major risk in enterprise AI is granting the model broad access via a generic service account, which could allow users to bypass security restrictions. We solve this by using OAuth 2.0 to perform user impersonation.

First, establish a confidential OAuth client in Snowflake to protect the client secret. The snippet below configures the security integration inside Snowflake:

To retrieve the generated client credentials needed for the Google Cloud configuration, run the following command in Snowflake:

Step 2: Data governance and access control

Apply the principle of least privilege by creating a dedicated role for your agent inside Snowflake.

IMPORTANT

  • The user context must have SELECT privileges on the physical tables backing the semantic view. Granting access only to the semantic view will cause runtime errors during query execution.
  • If granting direct access to base tables is not permitted by your security policy, place a Snowflake Secure View over the physical tables and build the Semantic View on top of it. Because Snowflake views execute with Owner's Rights, the user's GenAI role only needs SELECT privileges on the Secure View and Semantic View rather than the raw tables.
  • Snowflake OAuth tokens capture and bind to the user's DEFAULT_ROLE and DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE at the exact moment of authorization. If a user authorizes the connection before these defaults are configured, the session will be locked to the wrong role(role available at that time) and query execution will fail if the intended role will not have required privileges.
    • Set defaults(as shown below) prior to authorizing in Gemini Enterprise.
    • Authorize connection: Have the user perform the one-time OAuth authorization in Gemini Enterprise.
    • (Optional) Revert defaults: Once authorized, the user can safely revert their default role and warehouse in Snowflake back to their standard operational preferences.

Step 3: Provisioning the Cortex Agent and MCP server inside Snowflake

Next, create a governed Cortex Agent in Snowflake using your semantic view, then provision an MCP server that exposes the agent via the CORTEX_AGENT_RUN tool type. This approach delegates both SQL generation and query execution to Snowflake while enforcing the caller's OAuth identity and role permissions.

ISOLATION & GOVERNANCE NOTE: By using CORTEX_AGENT_RUN, query generation and execution remain fully contained within Snowflake's governed security boundary. Avoid exposing raw execution tools like SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL to external clients, as doing so introduces unnecessary security surface area and bypasses centralized Cortex Agent governance.

Step 4: Locating and constructing the MCP server URL

The ADK code requires the endpoint URL of your Snowflake-managed MCP server. Now that the server is provisioned, you must first grant access to the server, and then you can retrieve its exact endpoint URL using the following query in a Snowflake worksheet:

In the command output, inspect the metadata properties to locate the endpoint link. The URL is structured as follows:

Step 5: Connecting via Google ADK

With the MCP Server created and its URL resolved, write your agent code using the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK). In your Python code, define the unique identifier AUTH_ID (e.g. snowflake_oauth_conn) that the agent will use to extract user credentials.

NOTE: The Python snippet above represents a plain/vanilla version of the agent setup. Depending on your organization's specific requirements, you should add robustness on top of this template (e.g., custom error handling, structured schemas, custom prompts, configurations, and additional tool wrappers).

Step 6: Project structure and deployment

To deploy your ADK agent to Agent Runtime in Agent Platform, organize your files in the following directory layout:

  • File details
  • __init__.py: Exposes the root_agent object to the deployment CLI:
  • .env: Declares environment configuration:
  • requirements.txt: Specifies dependencies:

2. Deploying via the CLI

Rather than running complex custom Python scripts or manual container builds, you can deploy using the official Google Agents CLI (agents-cli). The CLI packages your code, sets up the server, and handles the deployment pipeline:

The CLI automatically handles the deployment lifecycle. Once complete, it outputs the unique project resource path (e.g., projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/reasoningEngines/RESOURCE_ID) which you will use to register the agent in the next step.

TIP: For more information and advanced configuration options for ADK agent deployment, refer to:

Step 7: Registering the custom agent in Gemini Enterprise

Once the agent code is ready and deployed, register the agent in the Google Cloud Console. Here, you will link the agent configuration and map the OAuth parameters retrieved from your Snowflake Security Integration.

  • Extracting the OAuth Endpoints from Snowflake

Run this query in Snowflake to extract the precise Token and Authorization endpoints:

In the results, locate the values for the following properties:

  • OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_ENDPOINT: Your Snowflake Authorization URI.
  • OAUTH_TOKEN_ENDPOINT: Your Snowflake Token URI.

2. Registration steps in Google Cloud console

  • Go to the Gemini Enterprise page in the console.
  • Select the application you want to register the agent with.
  • In the left navigation, click Agents, then click + Add agent.
  • Select Add for Custom agent via Agent Platform. The Authorizations setup displays.
  • Set up the Snowflake OAuth connection:
    • Click Add authorization.
    • Authorization name: Enter the exact ID you defined in your ADK code (e.g., snowflake_oauth_conn). This ensures the credentials map correctly to the code's AUTH_ID.
    • Client ID & Client secret: Input the credentials you retrieved from Snowflake using the SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS query.
    • Token URI: Input the exact token endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION.
    • Authorization URI: Take the authorization endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION and append ?response_type=code at the end (along with your client ID and scope query parameters, for example):

IMPORTANT

Ensure the Authorization URI ends with &response_type=code (or ?response_type=code if there are no other parameters). This parameter is required by Google Cloud to trigger the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.

  • Click Done, then click Next.

6. Configure the agent properties:

7. Click Create to complete registration.

Understanding identifier alignment

  • ADK Code AUTH_ID <==> Google Cloud Authorization Name: The AUTH_ID in your Python script must exactly match the Authorization Name/ID you input during console registration. Because we write code first, we reuse the code-defined identifier during registration.
  • Snowflake Security Integration Name (e.g. ): This is purely a Snowflake-side database object name. It does not need to match the Google Cloud Authorization Name or the AUTH_ID in your ADK Python code.

Get started

By uniting the Gemini model’s reasoning capabilities, ADK's orchestration, and Snowflake's governed data layer, you can safely bring AI to your data. This architecture provides an agentic assistant that respects your security perimeters while delivering business value.
